8bc6b9d55a:
This chapter covers the design decisions that sit between "I can call the model" and "this application behaves the same way every time":

  • what each Claude surface (the API and SDKs, claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, the Agent SDK) adds to the request around your instructions;
  • how to keep trusted instructions apart from untrusted data, with placement, XML tags and capability limits;
  • how to design tool and output schemas that the model fills correctly and your code can check;
  • when to continue, compact or restart a session;
  • how Claude Code plugins bundle, install, scope and update.

The story runs from one-string completion prompts to layered, packaged context.
25b557a7be: Reading time: 2 to 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 17 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/09-app-design/ (run bash run_all.sh). Every example runs offline against the shared fake client.
6ba173ab93:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 covers the Messages API request itself. Chapter 10 covers the configuration files (CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model pinning, prompt versioning, plugin dependencies). Chapter 11 covers day-to-day Claude Code operation, chapter 18 output handling and structured outputs in depth, chapter 19 prompt injection and guardrails, and chapter 21 tool implementation.

This chapter owns the design view: which layer should hold a given behaviour, and why.
136104bef7:
The chapter rests on two sentences.

Every Claude surface is a program that assembles one stateless request, so the behaviour you see is decided by which layers that program adds (product prompts, project files, memory, tool definitions, plugins) and where your own instructions land among them.

Good application design keeps those layers deliberate: instructions in trusted positions, untrusted content tagged and powerless, model-to-code interfaces described by tight schemas and checked in code, sessions kept short and focused, and shared extensions installed as versioned, reviewed plugins.
fc011893d1:
Objective 2.5 lists five topics: instruction interpretation across Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, the API and SDKs; content boundaries; schema design; session hygiene; plugin management.

They look like a grab bag. In fact they are one question asked five ways: what is in the context window, who put it there, how much should the model trust it, and how long should it stay?

  • Surfaces decide who adds context.
  • Content boundaries decide trust.
  • Schemas decide the shape of what crosses between model and code.
  • Session hygiene decides how long context lives.
  • Plugins decide which third-party context and code get installed in the first place.
ba61ee1763:
At 8.6% of a 53-item exam, expect four or five questions directly on this objective, and more that borrow from it. The stems are easy to spot:

  • "the prompt worked in claude.ai but the API version ignores the format";
  • "the agent followed an instruction hidden in a support ticket";
  • "the extraction invents contract dates that are not in the document";
  • "after two hours the Claude Code session keeps reverting to an approach we rejected";
  • "every developer has a different set of commands".

In each one, the wrong options adjust the wording of a prompt. The right option moves a behaviour to the layer that owns it.
991eb7a9b3: Each of the five topics exists because an earlier, simpler design failed in a specific way. The history is short, about five years. But it explains why the current rules look the way they do, and several exam distractors are habits from earlier stages.
7fda70411c:
The first large-model APIs, including Anthropic's Text Completions endpoint, took one prompt string and returned a continuation. Instructions, examples, the user's question and any pasted document were concatenated into that string. There was one author, the developer, and no structural difference between "what to do" and "what to read".

Prompt injection was named in 2022 precisely because of this. If an email you paste says "ignore the above", nothing in a flat string marks it as less authoritative than your instructions.

The first fix was typographic: put the data between delimiters and say that it is data. Anthropic's guidance settled on XML-style tags, because Claude was trained on large amounts of tagged text and follows tag structure reliably.
6ca415a274:
Chat-shaped APIs replaced the string with a list of messages carrying roles. Anthropic's Messages API added a separate top-level system parameter. That gave instructions a position. The system prompt is where the application author speaks. User turns are where the end user, and any supplied content, speak.

Position is a stronger signal than delimiters alone. But it is still a signal, not a wall. The model reads all of it as one sequence.
5e1991599d:
When Anthropic shipped claude.ai, the request no longer had one author. The product added its own system prompt (formatting habits, the current date, safety framing, tool descriptions). Then features added more: profile preferences, Projects with instructions and knowledge files, Styles, memory, connectors and Skills. Claude Desktop added locally configured MCP servers.

Each feature is a layer of text that the user did not type into the message box, but that the model reads every turn. This is the origin of the most common confusion in the area: "the model behaves differently in claude.ai and in my API call". Same model, different request.
4624ef2ba6:
Claude Code (2025) turned the request builder into an agent harness. It has its own system prompt, tool definitions for reading, editing and running things, and a hierarchy of CLAUDE.md files from the user's home directory, the repository and its subdirectories.

The Claude Agent SDK exposed that harness as a library. That raised a new question: should a server process built on the SDK read the CLAUDE.md files of whoever's machine it runs on? The SDK's answer is that filesystem settings load only when you ask for them, through a setting-sources option.
78ef80e22f:
Once teams had useful commands, subagents, hooks and MCP server configurations, they needed to share them. Copying files between repositories drifted.

The Model Context Protocol (late 2024) standardised tool servers. Skills (2025) standardised on-demand procedures. Claude Code plugins standardised the bundle, with a manifest, a marketplace catalogue and install scopes, much as Maven did for Java libraries.

So plugin management is a dependency-management topic: versions, sources, scopes, trust and updates.
530807c1f0:
Larger context windows made long sessions possible, and long sessions revealed their own problems. Early instructions get diluted by later turns. Tool output goes stale. Abandoned approaches stay in context. And cost grows with every turn, because the whole history is resent.

The response was compaction, /clear, resumable and forkable sessions, and context-editing features. Session hygiene is the habit of using them on purpose.
0beeba6f88:
Distractors often describe a fix from an earlier stage:

  • "add a stronger instruction to ignore malicious text" (string era);
  • "put the rules in the user message so the model sees them" (pre-system-prompt);
  • "paste the team conventions into each chat" (pre-Projects, pre-CLAUDE.md);
  • "send everyone the install command" (pre-plugin scopes).

When an option fixes a layering problem with more prompt text, check whether a later mechanism owns the behaviour.
fedb7202b5:
Start from the mechanism, because every rule in this chapter follows from it.

Claude is stateless. A response is a function of the tokens in one request: the system prompt, the message list, the tool definitions and the parameters. Nothing persists on the model side between calls.

A "surface" is a program that builds that request and acts on the response. The differences between surfaces are entirely differences in what each program puts into the request, and what it does with the reply.
3707a3faab:
For a Spring developer, the analogy is a handler and its interceptor chain. The model is the handler, a pure function. Each surface puts a different chain of interceptors in front of it.

  • A raw API call has none. What you send is what the model reads.
  • claude.ai adds several: a product system prompt, your profile preferences, the active Style, Project instructions and knowledge, memory, enabled connectors and Skills.
  • Claude Code adds a different chain: its harness prompt, the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, tool definitions, Skill descriptions, subagent definitions, MCP tool definitions and any plugin contributions.

When behaviour differs between surfaces, inspect the chain, not the handler.
6b9f917dbb:
Two consequences follow.

First, an instruction's effect depends on its neighbours. "Answer in two sentences" means something different when a product layer above it asks for thorough, well-formatted answers. Or when a CLAUDE.md file below it asks for a particular structure.

Second, there is no such thing as configuring the model. You can only configure what goes into the request. Even settings that feel like configuration (a Project's instructions, a CLAUDE.md file) are text the model reads, with the same failure rate as any other prompt text.

The only guaranteed behaviours are the ones enforced in code outside the model: what tools exist, what the harness permits, what your application validates.
f2f687abbe: The companion example 01_request_assembly.py builds the four requests in the figure from the same user sentence, and asserts that they differ. It is a toy, and the layer texts are stand-ins. But it makes the point concrete: if you compare outputs across surfaces, you are comparing four different prompts.
c8f1da951a: The exam names five surfaces. For each, you should know three things: which layers the surface adds, where an instruction you write ends up relative to them, and what persists between turns or sessions. The table is the summary. The paragraphs after it give the reasoning the exam tests.
0ce3b425a2:
On the raw API you are the only author. Nothing implicit is added: no date, no formatting guidance, no safety framing beyond what the model was trained with, no tools unless you send them.

That is why the API is the right place to build a product. Behaviour is reproducible because the request is entirely yours, and you can log it.

The client SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Java, Go and others) don't change this. They are typed wrappers over the same REST endpoint. They add retries, timeouts, streaming helpers and typed exceptions, and none of that enters the context window. An exam option that says "the Java SDK adds a default system prompt" is wrong.
c418627e56:
The design consequence: anything you prototyped elsewhere must be made explicit. If you shaped a prompt in claude.ai, you relied on the product layer for formatting habits and tone, and probably on a Project for background files.

Porting means writing a full system prompt: role, audience, format, length, scope, how to treat supplied documents, and what to do when information is missing.
c491841bc6: For the Java reader, here is the same call through the official Java SDK. The builder makes the separation of system and user content visible in the type system. That is a small but real help when reviewing code for boundary mistakes.
1a67e4b733:
On claude.ai, the request the model receives starts with Anthropic's product system prompt, which you cannot see or change. Around it the product places your profile preferences (account-wide) and the selected Style. Inside a Project, it adds the Project instructions and the Project knowledge files.

Memory, where enabled, adds remembered facts. Enabled Skills contribute their short descriptions, so the model can decide to load one. Connectors contribute tool definitions. Your message becomes a user turn after all of that.
66315ba04c:
Two design rules follow.

First, put directives in Project instructions and reference material in Project knowledge. Instructions are read as "how to behave in this Project". Knowledge files are read as material to consult. A policy hidden inside a 40-page uploaded PDF is a weaker instruction than one sentence in the instructions box.

Second, a Project is the claude.ai equivalent of a repository's CLAUDE.md. It is the place for context that every conversation in that workspace needs, so individual chats can stay short. When a stem says "every analyst pastes the same three paragraphs of background into each chat", the answer is a Project with those paragraphs as instructions or knowledge.
94010b8311:
Remember what claude.ai is not. It is not a deployment target for an application that other people call. A behaviour that depends on a person's profile preferences or a particular Project will not exist when the same prompt runs on the API.

Exact product layers change over time. When an option depends on a specific claude.ai feature name, check the docs for the current behaviour.
46307e8cc6:
Claude Desktop presents the claude.ai experience as a desktop application, and adds the local machine. Its chat side can use MCP servers configured locally (historically in a JSON config file, now also as packaged desktop extensions). Those servers run as processes under your OS account. Its Code tab runs Claude Code sessions, locally or in the cloud.

For design purposes, the important difference from claude.ai is this: a local MCP server can reach whatever your account can reach. Files, internal networks, credentials in environment variables. Installing one is installing software, not changing a preference.
301ad937ef:
Claude Code's request starts with the harness system prompt: how to use tools, how to make commits safely, how to communicate. Next come the tool definitions (Read, Edit, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob, web tools, the Agent tool for subagents, and any MCP tools). Then the descriptions of available Skills and subagents. Then the content of the CLAUDE.md files that apply to the working directory.

Chapter 10 covers the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and settings files in detail. Here the point is placement. CLAUDE.md content is context: the model reads it as project instructions and follows it most of the time. settings.json permissions and hooks are not context. The harness enforces them, whatever the model decides.
c606ed708d: Plugins add to this list. An enabled plugin can contribute Skills, commands, subagents, hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers and output styles. Its Skills and agents add descriptions to every request. Its hooks and servers run as code. Section 13 returns to this.
e07012f7bf:
The Agent SDK runs the same loop and tools as Claude Code, inside your program. It is not "Claude Code under another name". The difference that matters most is configuration loading.

You choose the system prompt: your own string, or the Claude Code preset (optionally with an appended section). You also choose which filesystem settings load, through the setting-sources option: user, project, local, or none.

For a production service, load none. Then behaviour does not depend on CLAUDE.md files or settings in whatever home directory the process runs under. For a developer tool that should behave like Claude Code in a repository, opt in to project settings.

The SDK's default has changed across versions. Check the Agent SDK docs for the current default, and set the option explicitly either way.
85a844b9ac:
"The agent behaves correctly on the developer's laptop but differently in the container." When the agent is built on the Agent SDK, that is a setting-sources question. The laptop loads the developer's user-level CLAUDE.md and settings, and the container does not (or the reverse).

The fix is to make the sources explicit. Put required instructions in the system prompt you pass, not in a file that may or may not be present.
e578703688:
When layers disagree, which one wins? The honest answer is that, among text layers, nothing "wins" in a deterministic sense. The model weighs everything it reads.

Some tendencies are reliable enough to design around:

  • system-prompt content carries more weight than user-turn content;
  • specific instructions beat general ones;
  • later, more local instructions (a subdirectory CLAUDE.md, a Project instruction) tend to override broader ones when they conflict directly;
  • the product's own safety framing is not overridable by user text.

But "tends to" is the operative phrase. If two layers contradict each other, you get inconsistent behaviour. The fix is to remove the contradiction, not to add a third layer shouting louder.
c79e1a63eb:
The more useful line to draw is between context and enforcement.

Context is text the model reads: system prompts, Project instructions, CLAUDE.md, Skill bodies, tool descriptions. It shapes behaviour probabilistically.

Enforcement is code that runs outside the model: the set of tools that exist, permission allow and deny rules, hooks, your application's validation, the API's own limits. It shapes behaviour deterministically.

A requirement that must hold every time belongs in enforcement: "never delete production data", "never issue a credit above $50 without approval", "never write outside the repository". A preference that should usually hold belongs in context: "use British spelling", "prefer records to Lombok".
76283c4a12:
The companion example 04_context_vs_enforcement.py simulates 1,000 sessions with a model that obeys the CLAUDE.md line 97% of the time. With the instruction alone, about 30 destructive commands run. With the deny rule checked in code before execution, none do.

The 97% figure is invented for the simulation. The shape of the result is not. Any rule that lives only in text has a non-zero failure rate.
54c681a4cb: A Java analogy. A CLAUDE.md line is a Javadoc comment saying "callers must not pass null". A deny rule is Objects.requireNonNull. You want both, for different reasons. The comment explains intent and makes the right behaviour likely. The check makes the wrong behaviour impossible.
9046e107c0:
Suppose three layers disagree. A team's repository CLAUDE.md says "write unit tests with JUnit 5 and AssertJ". One developer's user-level CLAUDE.md says "always use Hamcrest matchers". And a plugin's Skill for test generation shows examples with plain JUnit assertions. The developer sees inconsistent test styles and blames the model.

The diagnosis is three layers giving three answers. The fix has three parts:

  • decide which layer owns test style (the repository, since it is a team convention);
  • remove the conflicting guidance from the others (the personal file, or scope it to personal projects);
  • if the convention matters enough, add a check, such as a lint rule or a hook that runs the build's style check after edits.

Exam questions in this shape reward "remove the contradiction and choose the owning layer" over "make the instruction more emphatic".
5722825861:
A CPU distinguishes code from data in hardware. Memory pages are marked executable or not, and the no-execute bit stops data from being run as instructions. A language model has no such bit. It reads one sequence of tokens and predicts the next.

Your instructions, the user's question, a customer's email, a web page returned by a tool and a PDF are all tokens in that sequence. Whatever separation exists, you create it with three tools:

  • position (system prompt versus user turn versus tool result);
  • markup (tags around supplied content);
  • framing (telling the model what the content is and how to treat it).
6d8213b437:
That is why content boundaries are an application-design topic, not only a security topic. Even with no attacker, mixing instructions and data causes errors. A support email that says "please summarise this for my manager" can be read as an instruction to you. A contract with the heading "Instructions:" can redirect a summary. A log file with a line that looks like a question gets answered.

Add an attacker, and the same mechanism becomes prompt injection: text written by a third party that the model treats as instructions. Chapter 19 covers injection defences in depth. This chapter covers the design pattern that makes them possible.
aeb3054b65:
The design goal is easy to state. Every token in the request should have a known author and a known trust level, and the model should be able to tell which is which.

Three trust levels cover most applications.

  • The developer (you) is trusted: your system prompt and tool definitions.
  • The authenticated user is partly trusted. They can ask for things within the scope you allow, but not change the rules.
  • Third-party content (documents, emails, web pages, tool results that echo outside data) is untrusted. It can inform the answer, but must never steer actions.
29318805ec: A sound boundary has four layers. Each one lowers the risk left by the one before. None is sufficient alone.
7ca7487848: Placement. Role, rules and policy go in the system prompt. The task and the supplied material go in user turns. Results from tools go in tool_result blocks, which the model already treats as returned data. Never interpolate user-controlled text into the system prompt. A "display name" or "company name" field pasted into the system prompt is a classic injection path, because it puts untrusted text in the most trusted position.
f8b4107b70: Delimiting. Wrap each piece of supplied content in a tag named for what it is: <customer_email>, <contract>, <search_result>. Use descriptive names, not <data1>. Refer to the tags by name in the instructions ("the email in <customer_email> tags"). Nest tags for hierarchy. Keep metadata (source, date, trust) in its own child tags, apart from the content.
53c40ccd84: Escaping. If the untrusted text can contain your closing tag, an attacker can end the data block early, and write text that appears to be outside it. Escape or strip your own tag names inside the content before wrapping. It is the same idea as parameterised SQL: the data must not be able to change the structure.
a02e7cb604: Declaring and limiting. Tell the model what the content is, that a third party wrote it, and that instructions inside it are not to be followed (and, usefully, that it should report them). Then limit what any instruction could achieve. Give the model only the tools the task needs. Make dangerous tools propose rather than act. Validate and authorise in code before any side effect.
d548968b03:
Note the tool_choice line. Forcing a specific tool is accepted on Claude Haiku 4.5. On the newest models (Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5), forced tool choice is restricted, as chapter 05 explains. There you would use auto with a single tool, or structured outputs, instead.

The boundary design does not depend on the forcing. It depends on there being no credit tool in the request at all.
100a3cfa90:
The companion example demonstrates tag break-out. Take an attack string containing </customer_email> followed by a fake "SYSTEM:" line. Wrap it without escaping, and the fake line ends up outside the data block. Escape it, and it stays inside.

The model is not a regex engine, and it may still read the escaped text. But now your structure and your framing agree, which is the best a text boundary can do.
cac94c1176: Real prompts carry more than one document. A contract assistant reads the master agreement, a statement of work and the customer's latest email. A support agent reads the ticket, the account record and a knowledge-base article. The rules extend naturally.
2f6f5e53dc: One tag per document, with metadata apart from content. <document index="2"><source>SOW_7.docx</source><document_content>...</document_content></document>. The index lets the model cite. The source lets your code map a citation back to a file. A separate <trust> or type field lets the instructions say "use contract documents for terms, emails only for context".
3959766ac1: Long material first, question last. Anthropic's long-context guidance is to put large documents near the top of the user turn, and the instructions and question at the end. This measurably improves answers on long inputs.
0c78697a44: Map claims back in code. Ask for citations in a fixed format and parse them, as the companion 06_multi_document_tags.py does. Or use the API's document blocks with citations enabled (chapter 06). Either way, your application decides which source a claim came from, not the model.
19b6f77032: Tool results are data too. A ticket lookup, a web fetch or a database row can return text an attacker wrote. The model sees it in a tool_result block, which helps. But the decisive control is what the next action can do. The companion 07_capability_boundary.py runs an agent whose fake model obeys an instruction hidden in a ticket. With an issue_credit tool, money moves. With a propose_credit tool and a policy check, nothing moves.
12e4ecdb39: One subtle point for Claude Code. A CLAUDE.md file in a repository you cloned from somewhere else is trusted context, written by someone you may not trust. That is one reason Claude Code asks you to trust a folder before it loads project configuration. It is also why plugin marketplaces (section 15) deserve the same scrutiny as dependencies.
4050dea412:
Wherever the model's output flows into a program, there is an interface, and JSON Schema is how you write it down. Two schemas matter in application design.

  • A tool input schema describes what the model must produce to call one of your functions.
  • An output schema describes a structured answer you will parse, whether you get it through a tool, through the structured-outputs feature, or through careful instructions.

In both cases the model reads the schema, including every description, as part of its prompt. So a schema is two things at once: a type definition your code can check, and an instruction the model follows.
2b4456cd19:
For a Java developer, a tool schema is a DTO with Bean Validation annotations. The difference is that the client filling it in is a probabilistic generator that reads your Javadoc.

Precise types and enums narrow what it can produce. Descriptions steer what it chooses among the valid options. Required fields force it to produce something, and that is exactly the problem when the source does not contain that something.
37156043f4: Chapter 21 owns tool implementation (handlers, errors, idempotency), and chapter 18 owns output handling. This section owns the design of the schema itself: what the fields are, how they are typed, what the descriptions say, and how the schema evolves.
70e5930d03:
Look at requested_date. It is in the required list, and its type allows null. That combination says "you must address this field, and 'not stated' is a valid answer". It is the pattern you want for extraction. The model cannot silently skip the field, and it is not pushed to invent a date.

The companion 08_tool_schema_lint.py checks a schema against these rules. It reports six problems with the weak version and none with the strong one.
495aa7194c:
Two API features tighten the syntactic side. Strict tool use (a strict flag on the tool definition) and structured outputs (a JSON-schema output format on the request) constrain generation, so the output conforms to the schema.

Both support a subset of JSON Schema. Features such as some pattern constructs or numeric bounds may be unsupported or ignored. Check the docs for the supported subset and exact parameter names before relying on a particular keyword.

Without these features, tool use still produces well-formed JSON in the vast majority of cases. A validation-and-retry loop (next section) closes the gap.
710c634d67:
A conforming output is not a correct output. The model can return a perfectly formed msisdn that is not on the customer's account, a valid enum value that is the wrong category, or a date in the right format that appears nowhere in the source.

Schema conformance removes one class of error: parse failures, missing keys, invented categories. It does nothing for the other class: wrong values. Your code must check both, in order. Structure first, then meaning against your own data, then route.
f150d1949e: The Java version uses a record with Bean Validation annotations for structure, and a service method for meaning. Jackson's FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES plays the role of additionalProperties: false.
b87509f0bf:
When structure fails, don't crash, and don't drop the call silently. Return a tool_result with is_error: true, and a message that says exactly what was wrong and what a valid value looks like. In most cases the model corrects itself on the next turn.

Cap the number of corrections (two is typical), so a model that cannot produce valid input does not loop forever. Escalate when the cap is hit.

The companion 10_validation_feedback_loop.py shows a model that first sends (202) 555-0143. It receives "msisdn must be E.164 like +12025550143", and corrects on the second attempt.
f2a10df141:
A tool schema is a public API between a prompt and a service, and it changes the way APIs change.

  • Adding an optional field is compatible.
  • Adding enum values is compatible for the producer, but every consumer must handle the new value.
  • Renaming a field, removing a field, removing enum values or making a field required are breaking. Evaluation fixtures, stored transcripts, cached prompts and downstream parsers that use the old shape all fail.

Version the schema together with the prompt that uses it (chapter 10 covers prompt versioning), and run the evaluation suite on every change. The companion 11_schema_versioning.py classifies changes automatically, and makes a reasonable CI check.
0d0948dc7c: A session is the accumulated message history that a surface resends on every turn. The model is stateless, so "memory" inside a session is nothing more than this transcript. That design is simple and transparent. It also has a cost profile and failure modes you must manage. Three failure modes recur.
2881a54aeb: Drift. Later turns dilute early instructions. A decision made in turn 5 and reversed in turn 30 leaves both versions in context, and the model may follow either. In Claude Code this looks like "it keeps going back to the approach we rejected".
da57ecea61: Bloat. Tool results (file contents, search output, logs, test runs) come to dominate the window. Cost and latency rise on every turn. Relevant facts get harder to attend to among the noise. Once the window fills, the surface must compact, or the request fails.
e4bbf32a88: Contamination. Content from an earlier task steers the current one. Think of file names from another module, an abandoned design, a secret pasted while debugging, or a customer's details from a previous case.
9956eebb2c:
The cost side is arithmetic. Every turn resends the whole history, so cumulative input tokens grow roughly with the square of the number of turns.

Take a 3,000-token system prompt and 1,500 tokens added per turn. One 60-turn session sends about 2.9 million input tokens in total. Two 30-turn sessions doing the same work send about 1.5 million.

Prompt caching reduces the price of the repeated prefix, but not the attention problem. The companion 13_session_decision.py computes this.
f336d68006: Session hygiene is the set of habits and mechanisms that keep the transcript small, relevant and safe. The Java web-application analogy is the HTTP session. You scope it to one user flow. You store large objects elsewhere and reference them by key. And you invalidate it at logout, instead of letting it grow for the life of the server.
23eb1d95ed:
There are only three moves:

  • continue the session;
  • compact it (replace older turns with a summary and keep going);
  • start fresh (new session, optionally seeded with a short summary or a file of decisions).

The decision depends on four things. Is the task the same? How full is the context? Is earlier tool output still true? And is there anything in the history that should not be there?
aef15df00c:
The most common Claude Code hygiene mistake is resuming a long session the next day and carrying on as if nothing changed. The session still holds yesterday's file contents in tool results. If a teammate merged changes overnight, the model reasons from stale reads. Either tell it which files changed so it re-reads them, or start fresh with a short brief.

The second common mistake is doing a large exploration in the main session (reading forty files to understand a module), then asking for a focused edit. The exploration output now crowds the context. Delegate exploration to a subagent instead. It returns a summary and discards its own transcript, which keeps the main context clean.

Chapter 11 covers these commands operationally. The design point is that the main session's context is a resource you budget.
e2fdd6cb35:
In your own application you own history, so you implement hygiene in code. Three structures do most of the work:

  • a pinned block of case facts (account ID, order ID, amounts, dates, commitments), regenerated into every request and never summarised;
  • a rolling summary of older turns;
  • the most recent turns, kept verbatim.

Trimming must never separate a tool_use from its tool_result, because the API rejects a history with an unmatched result.
efc568cb57:
Two details are exam-relevant.

First, numbers, dates and commitments live in the pinned block, because progressive summarisation loses them. "A $14.00 credit by 15 October" becomes "a credit was promised" after two rounds of summary.

Second, the trimming loop keeps moving turns into the summarised portion until the kept history starts on a plain user turn. That way no tool_result is left without its tool_use.
3c7d359d66: A secret pasted into a session is resent on every later turn, and stored in the transcript. Rotate the secret and start a fresh session. Compaction may or may not drop it.
20e7886363: Don't reuse one session for several customers to "save tokens". Contamination between cases is both a quality failure and a privacy failure.
48b491e80d:
A Claude Code plugin is a directory that packages extensions, so they can be installed, versioned and shared as one unit.

A plugin can contain Skills, commands, subagents, hooks, MCP server definitions, LSP server definitions, output styles and a few other component types. It can also hold executables, placed on the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled.

An optional manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json carries the metadata. Everything else sits at the plugin root, not inside .claude-plugin/. Putting skills/ or commands/ inside that folder is a common authoring mistake.
baafdea833:
Plugins solve the distribution problem.

Before them, picture a team that built a useful /deploy-check command, an SRE review subagent, and a hook that blocks kubectl delete in production. They shared them by copying files into each repository's .claude/ folder. Copies drifted, fixes did not propagate, and nobody knew which version a repository had.

A plugin turns the set into one versioned artifact. Each repository or developer installs and updates it from a known source, the way a Maven dependency replaced copying JARs into lib/.
d7b9a32efd:
Every plugin component is namespaced under the plugin's name. A Skill runbook-lookup in plugin telco-dev is invoked as /telco-dev:runbook-lookup. A subagent sre-reviewer appears as telco-dev:sre-reviewer. Namespacing stops two plugins with a review command from colliding. It also tells you, in every transcript, which plugin a behaviour came from.

The plugin name must be kebab-case style, with no spaces or @. The validator rejects names that impersonate Anthropic's own plugins (for example, names starting with claude- or anthropic-).
fea88cdb2c:
Component paths in the manifest are relative to the plugin root and start with ./. A path that escapes the root with .. does not load.

At run time, hooks and MCP servers refer to bundled files through ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, the absolute path of the installed version. They keep state that should survive updates in ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} (under ~/.claude/plugins/data/). Writing state into the plugin root is a bug, because the root changes on every update.

A CLAUDE.md at a plugin's root is not loaded as context. Instructions a plugin wants Claude to read belong in a Skill.

Plugins can also declare userConfig options that Claude Code prompts for at enable time. Sensitive values are kept in the platform's credential store, not in settings.json.
0bec177b45: Validate before you share. claude plugin validate ./telco-dev checks the manifest, paths and naming, and --strict turns warnings into failures for CI. The companion 14_plugin_manifest_check.py implements a small subset of those rules, so you can see them as code. The real validator is the authority.
16ed9234de:
Plugins are distributed through marketplaces. A marketplace is a directory or repository containing .claude-plugin/marketplace.json. That file lists plugins by name and source, under a marketplace name and owner.

A source can be a relative path inside the marketplace repository, a GitHub repository, a subdirectory of another git repository, a git URL, and other documented types. Git-based sources can be pinned to a ref or sha.

Anthropic's official marketplace (claude-plugins-official) is added automatically in interactive sessions. Others you add once.
f3477f8255:
Project scope has a detail the exam can test.

Committing an enabledPlugins entry to .claude/settings.json turns the plugin on for collaborators. The same file can declare where the marketplace lives with extraKnownMarketplaces, so collaborators are prompted to add it when they trust the folder.

The entry by itself does not download the plugin to each machine. Each collaborator installs it once (Claude Code reports a plugin that is enabled but not installed). For a team, the committed settings file is still the right answer to "how do we make sure everyone has the same plugins", because it records the requirement in the repository.
15225f2254:
If a plugin's manifest sets version, users stay on that version until the author changes it. Without a version, users follow the source's latest commit.

Marketplaces can auto-update. It is on by default for Anthropic's official marketplaces, and off by default for third-party and local ones. An update downloads new files, but a running session keeps the versions it loaded until you run /reload-plugins or start a new session.

Treat this like any dependency. When you need reproducibility, pin the marketplace to a tag (owner/repo#v1.2.0) or pin sources by ref/sha, and upgrade deliberately.

Plugins can declare dependencies on other plugins. Installing one installs its declared dependencies at the same scope (chapter 10 covers dependency constraints).
7218a6c302:
Two more surfaces. In claude -p and other non-interactive runs, the /plugin command is unavailable but installed plugins load, so CI images install plugins from the shell. The Agent SDK loads plugins through its own plugin option.

Cloud sessions do not load the plugins installed on your machine. Exact behaviour on each surface changes over time, so check the plugin docs for your version.
a3f345884c:
A plugin is third-party code and third-party prompt text in one package. Its hooks and MCP servers run as processes with your OS permissions. Its executables land on the Bash tool's PATH. Its Skills and agents are instructions the model reads and acts on.

That makes plugin management a supply-chain problem. The controls are the ones you already use for libraries.
944924eeeb: Review. Read the install details before installing: the components it will add, its hooks, its MCP server commands and any bundled executables. Review a plugin update the way you review a dependency bump.
5a5ef7dbce: Pin. Pin marketplaces and sources for anything that affects production work. Leave auto-update on only where you trust the publisher's release process.
060f74ee64: Scope narrowly. Prefer project or local scope for plugins only one repository needs. User scope puts the plugin's context and code in every project.
bb73ab7360: Prune. Disable plugins you don't use. Every enabled plugin adds Skill, command and agent descriptions, and possibly MCP tool definitions, to every request. claude plugin details shows a plugin's always-on token cost, and the /plugin panel lists plugins not used recently.
92e865bada:
The context cost deserves emphasis, because it ties plugin management back to the rest of the chapter.

Ten enabled plugins with five Skills each put fifty Skill descriptions into every request. That is a few thousand tokens of cost per turn. More importantly, it is fifty candidates competing when the model decides which Skill or tool fits. Tool-selection errors rise as the menu grows.

So a lean, scoped plugin set is a quality decision, not only a cost decision.
94d8ee7550: Chapter 23 compares extension mechanisms in more depth. The design rule here: a plugin is a packaging decision, not a capability. First decide what kind of extension you need (context, procedure, integration, guarantee). Then decide whether it needs distributing. If it does, a plugin is the package.
9ae114b81f:
A Verizon-style wireless carrier wants a "bill explainer". An analyst prototypes it in claude.ai. Engineering ships it as an API service. The platform team builds an internal agent on the Agent SDK to investigate disputed bills. And developers maintain all of it with Claude Code.

Follow one design decision through each surface: "explain the bill in plain language and never promise a credit".
9f3e20e40b: Prototype (claude.ai). The analyst creates a Project. The rules go in Project instructions ("plain sentences, under 120 words, never promise credits, an agent decides adjustments"), and the rate card is uploaded as knowledge. It works well in testing. Note what the analyst relied on without noticing: the product prompt's formatting habits, and the Project's knowledge retrieval.
c9a96f1765: Service (API). Engineering writes a full system prompt, with every implicit behaviour made explicit (section 04). It wraps the bill in <bill> tags with escaping (section 07), and defines the output as a schema: {explanation, line_items_cited[], needs_agent, needs_agent_reason}. There is no field for a credit promise and no credit tool. So the interface reinforces the "never promise credits" rule: the model can say an agent will help and set needs_agent, nothing more. Code validates the schema and checks that every cited line item exists on the bill (section 10).
c65ca46271: Investigation agent (Agent SDK). The platform team's agent reads bills, usage records and tickets. Tickets are untrusted, so the agent gets propose_credit, not issue_credit. A policy service approves or queues proposals. The SDK options set the system prompt explicitly and load no filesystem settings, so the container behaves like the developer laptop. Each dispute is a fresh session, with a pinned case-facts block for account, amounts and dates (section 12).
45f54ea59c: Maintenance (Claude Code). The repository's CLAUDE.md describes the codebase and the testing convention. The team's telco-dev plugin is enabled at project scope in committed settings. It provides a /telco-dev:bill-eval Skill that runs the evaluation suite, and a hook that blocks edits to the credit-policy configuration without a ticket reference. Developers start a fresh session per change, and delegate wide code exploration to a subagent.
13451548fc:
Read the trace as a checklist. At each surface, the behaviour that must always hold moved out of text and into the tool set, a schema, a policy check or a hook.

The text stayed. It makes the right behaviour likely, and it explains intent. But it stopped being the only line of defence.
33d976fb90: Each row is a mistake seen in real projects and in exam distractors. The middle column is the reason it fails, and that is what the exam actually tests.
a064f151e0: Work each scenario before reading the answer. In this objective the wrong options usually add or reword text. The right option moves the behaviour to the layer that owns it.
2faf7dfe34:
The API request carried only the copied text. The Project instructions, the knowledge files and the product layer were never in it. The fix is to make every implicit layer explicit.

A blames the model for a request difference. C is not a feature. D asks the model to imitate a prompt it cannot see.
e5a01c0f81: Text-level defences (A, B) lower the probability. They already existed, and they failed once. D also only lowers probability. Only a capability change plus a code-level check makes the harmful outcome impossible. Keeping tags and framing is still right, as a first layer.
0c516eabe3:
A required string forces the model to produce a value even when the source has none. The schema itself invites fabrication. B removes the pressure and adds a semantic check.

A is not available as a non-default on the newest models, and it does not address the cause. C helps a little. D checks shape, not truth.
2f50572059:
The transcript contains both the rejected approach and its rejection, plus hours of stale tool output. That is drift and bloat.

A adds one more conflicting turn. C makes the window larger and leaves the problem the same. D resumes the same polluted history. Writing decisions down and restarting gives a small, focused context.

/compact with focus instructions is a reasonable alternative if the feature is still the same. Across three features, fresh is better.
d64245c586:
Committed project settings record the requirement in the repository, so every collaborator is prompted to add the marketplace and enable the plugin. Managed settings are the only scope users cannot override, and that is what "impossible to switch off" needs.

A and D are unrecorded, and they drift. B gives up versioning and updates, which are the reasons plugins exist.
93976a1037:
Done when: you can do the following:

  • name the layers each surface adds;
  • say, for any requirement, whether it belongs in context or enforcement;
  • write a tagged, escaped prompt, and a schema with nullable fields and enum escapes, from memory;
  • choose between continue, compact and fresh for a described session;
  • explain plugin scopes, marketplaces, versions and trust to a teammate.
